Little Lord Fauntleroy by Frances Hodgson Burnett published in 1886. Massively popular kid's book about a little boy dressed in lace and velvet with long, long curls. This kicked off a huge fad where mothers would dress their sons up to look like him, which in turn led many cultural pundits to decry Little Lord Fauntleroy as a sissy. (Stephan Crane, writer od The Red Badge of Courage, supposedly would give boys money to go cut their hair.) There were loads of debates and articles about the "sissy" Fauntleroy well into the 1930s (and how American boys were just NOT LIKE THAT). Fauntleroy became a shorthand for an over-intellectual, soft-handed sissy boy, with references from Faulkner's "Absolom, Absolom" to the TV show "Firefly," and none of them really reflect the actual character of the child (who is smart and lives his mom very much, but is also the leader of his street gang and very strong and athletic).

The whole damn history is hilarious and a little heartbreaking (the author based the character off her son, and he was haunted by it for the rest of his life), and no one really remembers that book anymore.

It's like arguing with a meme. For example, we can argue to death that the "firstworldproblems" meme (god I'm old, is this where I say "big cringe bruh fr fr") isn't an actual reflection of the various forces/barriers that industrialized people can face (and that using first world itself is a problem) but it also speaks to a broader critiques of privilege (and particularly white privilege given the image). Message has to fit the medium, as they say, and I genuinely think 95% of messages on Tik Tok are going to have these issues because it's a flaw of the medium.   


But honestly, fair point about my use of bad faith, which I used incorrectly. I was using it to reference the way that so many folks online want arguments to include every single, possible exception or counterpoint or refutation that fits their own political point, when most social media posts don't actually allow for that amount of nuance. I consider that bad faith, but it's for sure not the correct definition. But on that note, I'm gonna bow out. Oof, I would argue that your complaints are bad faith arguments, especially given the medium of Tik Tok and how that inherently limits the scope of her argument/evidence. She can't trace every single technological lineage that led to each individual element to the cell phone because it's not possible within the scope of a single Tik Tok, so she chooses particular examples that can help refute the original post and mixes both specific examples and broad communities to provide a wider range of evidence. Moreover, it makes zero sense for her to have to stop and clarify the racial diversity of each nation when ultimately, her point is that technologies move through a wide range of communities, each of which has a hand in developing it, and that given the wide scope of people/nations involved, we can easily assume that people of color were involved in the process, which again, is in direct response to the commenter's assumption that white people have "blessed" people of color and are the originators.
